I am sixty-nine years old this year. I have been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a young bride, and I never went to school — I cannot read a single character. But I know my fields. I know which patch stays wet after rain and which dries out first. I watch what my neighbors do, especially Old Li’s family down the road, because their wheat always looks thick and green.

This year I have ten mu of land. Eight mu I will plant with winter wheat and then summer maize, one after the other, like everyone else in the village. That is my insurance — if the maize price drops, I still have wheat to eat and sell. The other two mu I will plant cotton. Cotton is more work, especially the spraying, but the price has been steady and my nephew helps me pick it in autumn.

For the wheat, I will rotary-till the soil in early October, the same as always. I buy improved wheat seed from the supply shop — about thirty jin per mu. I put down compound fertilizer and urea together; altogether it comes to about two big bags of nutrients per mu. I would rather put a little too much than too little, because a thin wheat crop means a hungry winter. I will irrigate three or four times: once when I plant, once at green-up if the spring is dry, once at jointing, and maybe once more at grain-filling if the sky gives us no rain. I spray insecticide and herbicide four or five times through the season. If the wheat looks yellow, I topdress more urea. I expect about five hundred kilograms per mu if the weather behaves.

For the summer maize, there is no time to waste after wheat harvest in early June. I plant directly into the stubble without tilling — no-tillage, the young people call it, but I just know we have only a few days before the rains stop. I buy hybrid maize seed, one package per mu. Maize does not need as much fertilizer as wheat; one bag of compound and a little urea is enough. I irrigate twice, maybe three times if it is very hot. Three pesticide sprays should do it. I hope for about five hundred kilograms per mu.

For the cotton, I rotary-till in April and plant improved cotton seed. Cotton needs more spraying than the grains — I spray ten or eleven times for bollworms and weeds — but the income is good. I irrigate two or three times. I expect around three hundred kilograms of seed-cotton per mu.

I keep some cash back for medicine and emergencies. I do not hire labor if my son and daughter-in-law can help at harvest. That is my plan.
